rules.name: Missing Content-Security-Policy
rules.description: The response does not define a Content-Security-Policy header. Without a CSP the browser will execute any injected script, turning otherwise low-impact injection bugs into full cross-site scripting.
rules.remediation_example: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'

rules.name: Missing Strict-Transport-Security
rules.description: The response does not define Strict-Transport-Security. Without HSTS the browser may fall back to plaintext HTTP, allowing network attackers to downgrade and intercept or modify traffic.

rules.name: Missing or invalid X-Content-Type-Options
rules.description: The response does not set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Without it browsers may sniff a different content type than declared and treat user-supplied content as executable script or style.

rules.name: Missing frame protection (X-Frame-Options / frame-ancestors)
rules.description: Neither X-Frame-Options nor a CSP frame-ancestors directive is present. The page can be framed by third-party sites, enabling clickjacking against authenticated users.

rules.name: Missing Referrer-Policy
rules.description: The response does not define Referrer-Policy. Full URLs, including sensitive path or query parameters, may leak to third-party origins through the Referer header.

rules.name: Missing Permissions-Policy
rules.description: The response does not define Permissions-Policy. Powerful browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation) remain available to embedded content and injected script.

rules.name: Information disclosure via server banners
rules.description: The response exposes framework or server version details in Server, X-Powered-By or similar headers. Version banners help attackers match known vulnerabilities to the deployment.
rules.remediation_example: Remove or genericize the Server and X-Powered-By response headers.

rules.name: Cookie missing HttpOnly flag
rules.description: A Set-Cookie response header does not include the HttpOnly attribute. Client-side JavaScript, including injected script, can read the cookie and exfiltrate session tokens.
rules.remediation_example: Set-Cookie: session=<value>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

rules.name: Cookie missing Secure flag
rules.description: A Set-Cookie response header does not include the Secure attribute. The cookie may be transmitted over plaintext HTTP and intercepted on the network.
rules.remediation_example: Set-Cookie: session=<value>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

rules.name: Cookie missing or weak SameSite attribute
rules.description: A Set-Cookie response header omits SameSite or sets SameSite=None without Secure. The browser will attach the cookie to cross-site requests, enabling cross-site request forgery on state-changing endpoints.
rules.remediation_example: Set-Cookie: session=<value>; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

rules.name: Overly permissive CORS policy
rules.description: The response allows cross-origin access that is wider than intended: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is '*' while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true, or the wildcard is combined with a dynamic origin reflection. Browsers then let any site read authenticated responses on the victim's behalf.
rules.remediation_example: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com  (explicit origin, never '*' with credentials)

rules.name: Debug or stack trace disclosure in response body
rules.description: The response body contains a language or framework error traceback (Python, Django, Flask/Werkzeug debugger, SQL errors) rather than a generic error page. Tracebacks reveal file paths, framework versions, source lines and sometimes local variable values.
rules.remediation_example: Return a generic error page and log the traceback server-side (DEBUG = False in Django/Flask).

rules.name: Redirect and URL-fetch parameters exposed to visitors
rules.description: A link or form on the page carries a query parameter whose name implies a redirect target or a server-side fetch (url, redirect, next, target, dest, return_to, callback, continue, image, fetch). Such parameters steer where the browser or server goes next, so without an allow-list they become open-redirect and SSRF entry points.
rules.remediation_example: Accept only relative paths, or validate the destination against an allow-list of known hosts before redirecting or fetching.

rules.name: Directory listing or sensitive file content exposed
rules.description: The response body is an auto-generated directory index ('Index of /') or contains file content that should never be served, such as environment assignments (DB_PASSWORD=, SECRET_KEY=), a PEM PRIVATE KEY block, a .env file listing or a CI credential variable. Any visitor can read files the operator intended to keep internal.
rules.remediation_example: Disable auto-indexing (autoindex off / Options -Indexes) and deny requests for dotfiles, backups and .env paths at the web server.
